objective.title: Separate Cyrillic letters from Latin look-alikes

steps.title: Shape traps
steps.body: These printed letters often fool Latin-alphabet readers: В, Н, Р, С, У, Х. Name the Cyrillic identity. Read this as a review-pending explanation. Worked examples come before the guided choice, and the independent check is separate. A wrong answer returns to this contrast. Activity is not demonstrated ability.

steps.title: Guided contrast
steps.body: These printed letters often fool Latin-alphabet readers: В, Н, Р, С, У, Х. Name the Cyrillic identity. Choose once with the explanation still in view. This is practice, not the independent check.

steps.body: Identity check.

steps.title: Н is not H

steps.title: С is not C

steps.title: В, У, and Х

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin P. What is it?
items.feedback: Shape overlap with Latin P is a recognition trap. This is Cyrillic Р, not English P.

items.feedback: Х is a Cyrillic letter, not Latin X.

items.feedback: Р is the Cyrillic letter, even when the shape looks like Latin P.

steps.title: Guided contrast
steps.body: Ь, Ъ, and Й need special attention. Do not invent a spoken vowel for the signs. Choose once with the explanation still in view. This is practice, not the independent check.

steps.body: Identity check.

steps.body: Identity check.

items.prompt: What is the printed mark Ь?
options: A vowel you pronounce by itself
A mark, not a standalone vowel
items.answer: A mark, not a standalone vowel
items.feedback: Ь is a sign, not a vowel letter you read alone.

items.prompt: What is the printed mark Ъ?
options: The hard sign, not a vowel
items.answer: The hard sign, not a vowel
items.feedback: Ъ is the hard sign. It is not a spoken vowel and it is not Ь.

items.prompt: What is the printed letter Й?
options: A consonant letter, not a vowel
items.answer: A consonant letter, not a vowel
items.feedback: Й is not a vowel you read alone and it is not the soft sign.

items.prompt: What does this sign do?

It is the Latin letter b

items.feedback: Ь and Ъ are signs. Do not invent a spoken vowel for them.

steps.title: Read the admitted grouping sentence
steps.body: The frozen page says: So, in Russian, nouns have an intrinsic property called 'gender', which comes in three types: masculine, feminine, and neuter. An ending is not a substitute for the admitted record.

steps.title: Recorded masculine nouns
steps.body: These admitted records are listed as masculine. стол — table. дом — house. го́род — town. брат — brother. The admitted record for друг — friend is also masculine. Learn this recorded label; an ending is not a substitute for the record.

steps.title: Recorded feminine nouns
steps.body: These admitted records are listed as feminine. кни́га — book. вода́ — water. шко́ла — school. рабо́та — work. The admitted record for дверь — door is feminine. Learn this recorded label; do not guess the gender of another word from its ending.

steps.title: Four records in the third group
steps.body: These admitted records are listed as neuter. окно́ — window. письмо́ — letter. молоко́ — milk. мо́ре — sea.

steps.title: Two records the page still places in the first group
steps.body: дя́дя and мужчи́на decline like nouns ending in -а, and they are masculine. Say decline for these nouns. Do not say they conjugate.

steps.title: Review the admitted noun genders
steps.body:
The frozen page says: So, in Russian, nouns have an intrinsic property called 'gender', which comes in three types: masculine, feminine, and neuter. An ending is not a substitute for the admitted record.

These admitted records are listed as masculine. стол — table. дом — house. го́род — town. брат — brother. The admitted record for друг — friend is also masculine. Learn this recorded label; an ending is not a substitute for the record.

These admitted records are listed as feminine. кни́га — book. вода́ — water. шко́ла — school. рабо́та — work. The admitted record for дверь — door is feminine. Learn this recorded label; do not guess the gender of another word from its ending.

These admitted records are listed as neuter. окно́ — window. письмо́ — letter. молоко́ — milk. мо́ре — sea. 

дя́дя and мужчи́на decline like nouns ending in -а, and they are masculine. Say decline for these nouns. Do not say they conjugate.

steps.body: The infinitive говори́ть names this entry. Match each supplied present form to its person: I: говорю́; you (one familiar person): говори́шь; he: говори́т; we: говори́м. steps.title: Identify the noun’s case role
steps.body: In the supplied Муж говорит, the husband is the subject and the talking verb states its action. The subject noun is nominative. Recognizing the English sentence meaning is useful, but the role check asks whether the noun is a subject or direct object. Do not guess nominative merely because a case is unfamiliar.

steps.title: Separate the subject from its description
steps.body: In Поезд старый, the train is the subject noun and old is its predicate description. This present property clause has no overt Russian copula. The noun’s case role is nominative subject, not accusative direct object. A dictionary-looking noun or familiar translation alone does not identify its role in every construction.

steps.title: Apply the distinction to a different supplied noun
steps.body: Студент новый supplies a second independent property clause: the student is the subject noun, and new describes that subject. Its case role is nominative subject. Keep Муж говорит — The husband is talking and Поезд старый — The train is old as correct sentence meanings; the optional reference choices do not demonstrate this case role. These supplied examples are deliberately taught, not unseen evidence or unrestricted productive case use. Other constructions have nominative predicate nouns; not every nominative noun is a subject.

steps.title: Admitted possession, objects, and direction
steps.body: Proposed Unit 6 uses frozen records for possession, objects, and direction. Qualified review is pending.
steps.bookDirection: Open Lesson 6 in the copy you own. The app records do not replace that lesson.

steps.title: My: agreement with the noun
steps.body: In мой стол, стол is masculine singular. In моя собака, собака is feminine singular. Both phrases mean my plus a noun, but the Russian form of my changes to match the noun.

steps.title: Match gender, number and case
steps.body: Possessives such as мо́й and тво́й agree with the noun they describe in gender, number and case. Choose the form from the noun, not from the gender of its owner. Start with the nominative forms below, then compare the feminine accusative example.

steps.title: Our: a worked case change
steps.body: Наш means our; Ваш means your. In the worked phrase на́ша сестра́, both words are feminine singular nominative. To put this phrase in the direct-object accusative, change both words: на́ша сестра́ becomes на́шу сестру́. Keep the same noun and feminine singular agreement. на́шего бра́та changes the referent, and на́ши is plural.

steps.title: Masculine and feminine forms
steps.body: In the nominative singular, мо́й is masculine and моя́ is feminine. For стол choose мо́й; for собака choose моя́. The form follows the noun being described.

steps.title: Neuter and plural forms
steps.body: моё is the neuter singular nominative form of my. мои́ is the plural nominative form. A singular noun does not take the plural form in these choices.

steps.title: Your: masculine and feminine
steps.body: тво́й is masculine singular nominative; твоя́ is feminine singular nominative. Both mean your. To change the masculine form to the feminine form while keeping nominative singular, choose твоя́.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Choose the form that matches the noun. Then read why the other forms do not fit.

steps.title: Review the agreement rule
steps.body:
Possessives such as мо́й and тво́й agree with the noun they describe in gender, number and case. Choose the form from the noun, not from the gender of its owner. Start with the nominative forms below, then compare the feminine accusative example.

In мой стол, стол is masculine singular. In моя собака, собака is feminine singular. Both phrases mean my plus a noun, but the Russian form of my changes to match the noun.

In the nominative singular, мо́й is masculine and моя́ is feminine. For стол choose мо́й; for собака choose моя́. The form follows the noun being described.

моё is the neuter singular nominative form of my. мои́ is the plural nominative form. A singular noun does not take the plural form in these choices.

Наш means our; Ваш means your. In the worked phrase на́ша сестра́, both words are feminine singular nominative. To put this phrase in the direct-object accusative, change both words: на́ша сестра́ becomes на́шу сестру́. Keep the same noun and feminine singular agreement. на́шего бра́та changes the referent, and на́ши is plural.

тво́й is masculine singular nominative; твоя́ is feminine singular nominative. Both mean your. To change the masculine form to the feminine form while keeping nominative singular, choose твоя́.

items.feedback: стол is masculine singular, so the nominative form is мо́й.
distractorRationales: моя́ is feminine singular nominative; it does not agree with the masculine singular noun.

distractorDifference: моя́ is feminine singular nominative; it does not agree with the masculine singular noun.
assessment.whyAnswerDemonstratesObjective: стол is masculine singular, so the nominative form is мо́й.

на́ши is plural and does not mark the feminine singular object row.

на́ши is plural and does not mark the feminine singular object row.
assessment.whyAnswerDemonstratesObjective: The shown feminine nominative на́ша сестра́ agrees with the object-row phrase на́шу сестру́.

steps.title: One adjective, several forms
steps.body: An adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case. In хорошее письмо, the adjective describes a neuter singular noun. хоро́ший is the dictionary form: masculine singular nominative. The following forms belong to the same adjective meaning good.

steps.title: Two spelling conditions
steps.body: After ж, ц, ч, ш, or щ, an unstressed о in an ending is written е. That replacement is not a rule for every unstressed о. In хоро́шее, the unstressed ending after ш uses е. The и in хоро́шие follows a different spelling condition: write и rather than ы after ш. Spelling limits the letters in an ending; gender, number and case determine which form is needed.

steps.title: Gender and a worked case change
steps.body: хоро́шая is feminine singular nominative; хоро́шее is neuter singular nominative. In хоро́шая книга, both words are feminine singular nominative. To put the phrase in the accusative singular, change both words: хоро́шая книга becomes хоро́шую книгу. Keep the same noun and feminine singular agreement. хоро́шего друга is masculine animate; хоро́шие книги is plural.

steps.title: Singular, plural and dictionary form
steps.body: хоро́шие is plural nominative. To change хоро́шее from neuter singular nominative to plural nominative, choose хоро́шие. To go back to neuter singular, choose хоро́шее. To supply the dictionary form, choose хоро́ший. These choices test the requested form of the adjective; all the options are already correctly spelled.

capabilities.exactSpan: most adverbs are formed by removing the adjectival suffixes "-ий" "-а" or "-е" from an adjective, and replacing them with the adverbial "-о". For example, in Ukrainian, "швидкий", "гарна", and "смачне" (fast, nice, tasty) become "швидко", "гарно", and "смачно" (quickly, nicely, tastily), while in Russian, "быстрый", "хороший" and "прекрасный" (quick, good, wonderful) become "быстро", "хорошо", "прекрасно" (quickly, well, wonderfully).

objective.title: Recognize supplied singular and plural nominative noun forms

steps.title: Admitted plural and availability rows
steps.body: Proposed Unit 8 uses frozen plural and availability rows. Qualified review is pending.
steps.bookDirection: Open Lesson 8 in the copy you own. The app records do not replace that lesson.

steps.title: Distinguish one table from tables
steps.body: сто́л is singular nominative; столы́ is plural nominative. In the selected table sense, the plural refers to tables. The English notes beside these examples are dictionary labels, not plural English translations or complete sentences. Choose the plural form when the question requests plural nominative. Both the ending and the supplied stress matter; do not insert a new stress pattern.

steps.title: Keep lexical gender separate from plural agreement
steps.body: These checks select supplied nominative plural noun forms. Each noun retains its dictionary gender; plural adjective agreement does not require separate masculine, feminine and neuter plural endings. The source’s single plural agreement category is not a claim that nouns lose lexical gender. Gender alone is not a complete algorithm for unfamiliar plural endings or stress. Learn these supplied pairs rather than applying them to every noun.

steps.title: Recognize the town pair
steps.body: го́род is singular nominative; города́ is plural nominative in this supplied pair. Select the latter for towns. The plural ending differs from the table pair and its supplied stress is on the final syllable. These patterns are word-specific recognition evidence, not permission to generate an unlisted form.

steps.title: Recognize the book pair and its spelling
steps.body: кни́га is singular nominative; кни́ги is plural nominative. Select the latter for books. The supplied plural retains its stress. Its final vowel follows the stem’s last consonant, one of the seven spelling-rule letters taught in the later spelling session. This same correct book pair is reused there as reinforcement; earlier independent credit does not replace that later objective’s checks.

steps.title: Recognize the window pair and shifted stress
steps.body: окно́ is singular nominative; о́кна is plural nominative in the supplied dictionary pair. Select the latter for windows. Notice the supplied stress moves to the first syllable. An ending-only guess would lose part of the taught form; do not invent another accent or treat this pair as every neuter noun’s algorithm.

steps.title: Recognize the mom pair
steps.body: ма́ма is singular nominative; ма́мы is plural nominative. Select the latter for moms in the supplied sense. The ending changes while the supplied stress stays in place. A feminine dictionary label alone does not prove every feminine noun has this ending.

steps.title: Recognize the house pair
steps.body: до́м is singular nominative; дома́ is plural nominative in the supplied house sense. Select the latter for houses. Preserve the source stress shift. The dictionary’s English house/home labels identify a sense; they are not a plural translation of the Russian form.

steps.title: Recognize the word pair within the taught scope
steps.body: сло́во is singular nominative; слова́ is plural nominative in the supplied word sense. Select the latter for words. Preserve its final stress. The seven pairs in this lesson cover several endings and stress patterns, but do not establish an unrestricted productive plural algorithm or meanings in every case. A missed choice returns to all cards and fourteen original worked forms.

го́род is singular nominative; города́ is plural nominative in this supplied pair. Select the latter for towns. окно́ is singular nominative; о́кна is plural nominative in the supplied dictionary pair. Select the latter for windows. Notice the supplied stress moves to the first syllable. ма́ма is singular nominative; ма́мы is plural nominative. Select the latter for moms in the supplied sense. The ending changes while the supplied stress stays in place. A feminine dictionary label alone does not prove every feminine noun has this ending.

до́м is singular nominative; дома́ is plural nominative in the supplied house sense. Select the latter for houses. Preserve the source stress shift. The dictionary’s English house/home labels identify a sense; they are not a plural translation of the Russian form.

сло́во is singular nominative; слова́ is plural nominative in the supplied word sense. Select the latter for words. Preserve its final stress. The seven pairs in this lesson cover several endings and stress patterns, but do not establish an unrestricted productive plural algorithm or meanings in every case. steps.title: Singular and plural forms
steps.body: Adjectives agree with their nouns in gender, number and case. In хорошее письмо, the adjective describes a neuter singular noun. хоро́ший is the dictionary form: masculine singular nominative. This lesson compares singular and plural nominative forms, then explains the spelling in the retained plurals.

steps.title: The seven-letter spelling rule
steps.body: After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, or щ, write и rather than ы. The seven-letter condition is required. This rule applies to the spelling of noun and adjective endings. In кни́ги, и follows г; in хоро́шие, и follows ш. The rule controls spelling, but the question determines the required gender, number and case.

steps.title: A worked noun plural
steps.body: For these nominative checks, кни́га means book in the singular and кни́ги means books in the plural. To form this plural, replace the singular ending with the plural ending: кни́га becomes кни́ги. The stem ends in г, so the seven-letter rule requires и. To return to singular nominative, choose кни́га.

steps.title: Two plural forms, different patterns
steps.body: кни́ги is plural nominative in this lesson. дни is also plural nominative and means days. Its и does not follow a letter in the seven-letter set, so дни is not an example of that spelling replacement. Not every plural ending in и comes from the seven-letter rule. Identify number from the requested form and context.

steps.title: Adjective number and dictionary form
steps.body: хоро́шее is neuter singular nominative; хоро́шие is plural nominative. To change the neuter singular form to plural nominative, choose хоро́шие; to return to neuter singular, choose хоро́шее. For the masculine singular dictionary form, choose хоро́ший. All these options are correctly spelled: the questions test form recognition rather than choosing between correct and incorrect spellings.

steps.title: Choose one by gender
steps.body: один мальчик — one boy; одна девушка — one girl. For these singular counting examples, one agrees with the noun: masculine один and feminine одна. Both still mean one. Guided practice uses мальчик.

steps.title: Choose the form of two

steps.title: Start with the construction
steps.body: These basic counting examples use nominative phrases. The related noun-case pattern also applies in inanimate accusative contexts, with the appropriate noun form. Other sentence cases require numeral declension as well as noun declension. A count ending in one outside the teen exception uses a nominative singular noun in the shown basic phrases. один час — один час. два часа — два часа.

steps.title: Two, three and four
steps.body: A count ending in two, three or four outside the teen exception uses a genitive singular noun in the basic construction. This is a grammatical singular form even though the count is greater than one.

steps.title: Genitive plural counts
steps.body: Counts ending in zero or five through nine use genitive plural in the basic construction. The teen exception also uses genitive plural. Ten and sixteen therefore fit this pattern. пять часов — пять часов. двадцать один час — двадцать один час.

steps.title: Compound counts
steps.body: For a compound count, inspect the last two digits first. If they are 11, 12, 13 or 14, use genitive plural for the counted noun in the basic construction. Otherwise, the final digit selects the pattern: one, two-through-four, or zero/five-through-nine. Compare 21 and 22: their final digits select different noun cases; being larger than five is not enough to choose genitive plural. двадцать два часа — двадцать два часа. две девушки — two girls.

steps.title: Teen values and exceptions
steps.body: For a compound count, inspect the last two digits first. If they are 11, 12, 13 or 14, use genitive plural for the counted noun in the basic construction. Otherwise, the final digit selects the pattern: one, two-through-four, or zero/five-through-nine. All counts from 11 through19 use genitive plural here. For 15 through19 the final digit already leads to genitive plural;11 through14 override the one/two/three/four ending pattern. пять девушек — five girls. шестнадцать рублей — sixteen rubles.

steps.title: One and zero endings
steps.body: The example with 41 follows the final-one pattern and uses nominative singular for the counted noun. The example with 10 follows the zero-ending pattern and uses genitive plural. десять копеек — ten kopeks. сорок один год — forty-one years.

steps.title: Hundreds preserve the boundary
steps.body: The count 203 ends in 03, so final three selects genitive singular in the basic counting phrase. The count 213 ends in 13, so the teen exception selects genitive plural. пять лет — пять лет. двести три собаки — two hundred and three dogs.

steps.title: Compare the supplied hundreds
steps.body: For a compound count, inspect the last two digits first. If they are 11, 12, 13 or 14, use genitive plural for the counted noun in the basic construction. Otherwise, the final digit selects the pattern: one, two-through-four, or zero/five-through-nine. Compare the supplied 203 and 213 examples and the two kopeck examples. Count value and sentence construction govern the explanation. двести тринадцать собак — two hundred and thirteen dogs. Два́дцать две копе́йки — 22 kopecks.

steps.title: Identify the counting context
steps.body: These basic counting examples use nominative phrases. The related noun-case pattern also applies in inanimate accusative contexts, with the appropriate noun form. Other sentence cases require numeral declension as well as noun declension. In these basic examples, a final one outside the teen exception uses nominative singular; final two, three or four use genitive singular. один час — один час. три кошки — three cats.

steps.title: Check the teen exception
steps.body: For a compound count, inspect the last two digits first. If they are 11, 12, 13 or 14, use genitive plural for the counted noun in the basic construction. Otherwise, the final digit selects the pattern: one, two-through-four, or zero/five-through-nine. All teen counts in the supplied basic examples take genitive plural.

steps.title: Genitive plural examples
steps.body: Five and sixteen both use genitive plural in these counting examples. The complete value matters: a compound count ending in one outside the teen exception has a different pattern. пять девушек — five girls. шестнадцать рублей — sixteen rubles.

steps.title: A sentence outside the basic pattern
steps.body: The I saw two friends sentence has an animate accusative object. Both the numeral and noun are declined; do not classify it with the basic nominative/inanimate accusative rule. The one-cat example below instead states existence in the basic nominative context. Я видел двух друзей — I saw two friends. Есть оди́н кот — There is one cat.

steps.title: The possessor and the possessed thing
steps.body: In the simple possession pattern shown here, the possessor after the possession preposition is genitive. The thing possessed is nominative. The schematic slot in the first example represents that possessed thing. У меня есть Х — I have X. У вас есть сын? — Do you have a son?

steps.title: Possession versus absence
steps.body: A simple positive possession line places the possessed thing in the nominative. An absence line places the absent thing in the genitive. Decide whether the whole shown line affirms or denies possession.

steps.title: Positive statements and questions
steps.body: The son examples keep the same simple possession pattern in a statement or question: genitive possessor and nominative possessed thing. The form of a question does not turn the noun into an absence construction. Да, у меня есть сын. — Yes, I have a son. У твоего́ му́жа есть оди́н друг — Your husband has one friend.

steps.title: Keep quantity and absence separate
steps.body: The many-friends example includes a quantity expression. Quantity patterns are separate from the simple nominative possessed thing in the son checks. The no-son example below denies possession and uses the genitive for the absent thing. У моего нового мужа есть много друзе́й — My new husband has many friends. У меня́ нет сы́на — No, I don't have a son.

steps.title: Another absence example
steps.body: The no-money example also denies possession. Choose the genitive absence explanation, rather than the simple positive possession explanation. У моего́ бра́та нет де́нег — My brother doesn't have any money.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Read the whole shown line, then choose the complete case explanation. A missed check returns to all teaching and examples.

steps.title: Identify absence
steps.body: In an absence line, the absent thing is genitive. An absence line may describe what a person does not have or what does not exist at a place. У меня́ нет сы́на — No, I don't have a son. Нет рестора́нов — There are no restaurants.

steps.title: Choose a complete case explanation
steps.body: The absence construction uses a genitive noun for the absent thing. The simple positive possession construction instead uses a genitive possessor and a nominative possessed thing. Choose from the meaning and construction of the whole supplied line.

steps.title: Apply the absence pattern
steps.body: Both negative examples below use the genitive for the absent thing. Keep the absent thing separate from any possessor or place mentioned in the line. В Москве́ нет ста́рых зда́ний — There are no old buildings in Moscow. У моего́ бра́та нет де́нег — My brother doesn't have any money.

steps.title: Compare with positive possession
steps.body: The positive son example below affirms possession. Its possessed noun is nominative, so the genitive absence explanation does not classify this line. Да, у меня есть сын. — Yes, I have a son.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Read the whole shown line, then choose the complete case explanation. A missed check returns to all teaching and examples.

items.prompt: Which admitted line is the first-person singular future?
items.feedback: Я бу́ду говори́ть is the first-person singular future: the subject means I, and the future auxiliary agrees with one speaker. Мы бу́дем говори́ть is first-person plural, meaning we. The imperfective infinitive stays the same while the subject and auxiliary change.
distractorRationales: Мы бу́дем говори́ть has a first-person plural subject and auxiliary, rather than the requested first-person singular future.

distractorDifference: Мы бу́дем говори́ть has a first-person plural subject and auxiliary, rather than the requested first-person singular future.
assessment.whyAnswerDemonstratesObjective: Я бу́ду говори́ть is the first-person singular future: the subject means I, and the future auxiliary agrees with one speaker. Мы бу́дем говори́ть is first-person plural, meaning we. The imperfective infinitive stays the same while the subject and auxiliary change.

items.prompt: Which admitted line is the second-person plural future?
items.feedback: Вы бу́дете говори́ть is the second-person plural future row: the auxiliary agrees with you in that row. This form can also address one person politely. Я бу́ду говори́ть is first-person singular and changes the person as well as the table number. The same imperfective infinitive follows each auxiliary.

Я бу́ду говори́ть is first-person singular and changes the person as well as the table number. The same imperfective infinitive follows each auxiliary.

items.feedback: Мы бу́дем говори́ть is the first-person plural future: the subject means we, and the future auxiliary agrees with that plural subject. Я бу́ду говори́ть is first-person singular, meaning I. Both use a future auxiliary plus the same imperfective infinitive; choose the plural line requested here.
distractorRationales: Я бу́ду говори́ть has a first-person singular subject and auxiliary, rather than the requested first-person plural future.

distractorDifference: Я бу́ду говори́ть has a first-person singular subject and auxiliary, rather than the requested first-person plural future.
assessment.whyAnswerDemonstratesObjective: Мы бу́дем говори́ть is the first-person plural future: the subject means we, and the future auxiliary agrees with that plural subject. Я бу́ду говори́ть is first-person singular, meaning I. Both use a future auxiliary plus the same imperfective infinitive; choose the plural line requested here.

objective.title: Recognize the two taught aspect pairs

steps.title: Admitted future, aspect, and row contrasts
steps.body: Proposed Unit 12 uses frozen records for future lines, aspect partners, indirect-object rows, spelling, and plural rows. Qualified review is pending.
steps.bookDirection: Open Lesson 12 in the copy you own. The app records do not replace that lesson.

steps.title: Aspect and time
steps.body: Aspect describes how an action is viewed, not when it happens. Imperfective can focus on an activity, repetition, or the fact that an action occurred without emphasizing its endpoint. Perfective presents an event with its boundary or result. Imperfective does not by itself mean unfinished. говори́ть is imperfective; сказа́ть is perfective. These infinitives do not specify tense on their own.

steps.title: The saying and telling pair
steps.body: Many Russian verbs are learned in an aspect pair, but not every verb has two words, and a pair is not automatic. говорить and сказать are context-dependent counterparts, not a universal pair for the English verb speak. For the saying/telling pair shown here, the perfective counterpart of говори́ть is сказа́ть; the imperfective counterpart of сказа́ть is говори́ть. These checks ask you to recognize this vocabulary pair, not choose aspect in a sentence.

steps.title: A worked doing and making pair
steps.body: де́лать is imperfective; сде́лать is perfective. Both concern doing or making. The perfective focuses on accomplishing the action; the imperfective can describe the activity or its occurrence without that focus. Given де́лать and a request for its perfective counterpart, choose сде́лать. говори́ть concerns speaking or saying and belongs to the other pair. Learn the shown pair rather than assuming every prefix changes only aspect.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Choose the counterpart from the saying/telling pair. Then compare its aspect and meaning with the other option.

objective.title: Choose the admitted past aspect line

steps.title: Admitted past aspect and report lines
steps.body: Proposed Unit 13 uses frozen records for past aspect lines, report labels, and infinitive partners. Qualified review is pending.
steps.bookDirection: Open Lesson 13 in the copy you own. The app records do not replace that lesson.

steps.title: Admitted lines
steps.body: The supplied lines я читал — I was reading and я прочитал — I read are both past-tense forms with masculine singular agreement. The line я читал is imperfective past; the line я прочитал is perfective past. The first presents reading as activity or process; the second presents it as a completed whole. These English labels describe the retained examples; they are not a rule matching every English past tense to one Russian aspect.

steps.title: Admitted instruction
steps.body: Do not treat English past progressive and simple past as a fixed Russian aspect code. The imperfective does not always mean the action was unfinished. An activity may have ended and still be described imperfectively when the focus is its process or occurrence rather than its endpoint. Recognize the requested aspect in these supplied choices; this is not unrestricted sentence production.

steps.title: Admitted lines
steps.body: чита́ть is the supplied infinitive; чита́л is its masculine singular past form. The dictionary label read names the recorded meaning and does not itself distinguish English past from infinitive. Compare the entire supplied forms. A question requesting masculine past asks for чита́л rather than feminine чита́ла; both past forms belong to the same imperfective verb.

steps.title: Admitted lines
steps.body: чита́ла is the supplied feminine singular past form of чита́ть. Compare it with masculine чита́л. This contrast changes gender agreement, not aspect. The pronoun I does not choose one past-tense gender for every speaker; these checks request a particular recorded form. steps.body:
The supplied lines я читал — I was reading and я прочитал — I read are both past-tense forms with masculine singular agreement. The line я читал is imperfective past; the line я прочитал is perfective past. The first presents reading as activity or process; the second presents it as a completed whole. These English labels describe the retained examples; they are not a rule matching every English past tense to one Russian aspect.

Do not treat English past progressive and simple past as a fixed Russian aspect code. The imperfective does not always mean the action was unfinished. An activity may have ended and still be described imperfectively when the focus is its process or occurrence rather than its endpoint. Я бу́ду рабо́тать is the supplied auxiliary-plus-imperfective future without that stated duration. The limit describes this work period, not necessarily completion of a task.
